analysis.one_liner: Requires the Education Department to vet student loan servicers' track records and make them fix their errors.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on June 7, 2024 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the Department of Education to scrutinize student loan servicers' past performance before hiring them, including consumer complaints, penalties, lawsuits, and their ability to help borrowers at risk of default. Once hired, servicers would have to fix their own mistakes: placing loans in forbearance without interest while a servicer error is being corrected, counting that time toward loan forgiveness, refunding overpayments, reimbursing fees, and cleaning up credit reports they damaged. It would also let the Secretary cancel contracts with servicers who misled the government, and order an independent study of how loan transfers and servicing errors hurt borrowers' credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers whose loans are mishandled. The bill targets servicer errors specifically: a borrower whose loan was put in the wrong status, charged the wrong amount, or wrongly reported delinquent would get the error corrected, the financial damage refunded, and the black mark removed from their credit report. Borrowers seeking Public Service Loan Forgiveness or income-driven repayment would not lose credit toward forgiveness because of a servicer's mistake. Borrowers who speak Spanish, Mandarin, Haitian Creole, or Arabic, and borrowers with disabilities, would get information in an accessible form.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal student loan borrowers hurt by servicer errors

how_it_helps.text: Before signing a servicing contract, the Education Secretary must evaluate the servicer's past performance: consumer satisfaction, customer service quality, error rates during loan transfers, any penalties the Department imposed for misconduct, and any legal action taken against it, including by states.

When a servicer identifies its own error, it must place the affected loans in administrative forbearance with no interest accruing, and that time must count toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness and income-driven repayment forgiveness as if the borrower had made payments.

Servicers must remedy financial harm from their errors: refund overpayments, reimburse fees like insufficient funds charges, and ensure credit reporting agencies remove negative information caused by the servicer's error.

The Secretary may revoke a servicer's contract if the servicer knowingly withheld information or made misrepresentations during the vetting process, after notice and a hearing, and the servicer must abide by that decision.

The Comptroller General (the nonpartisan investigative arm of Congress) must study how loan transfers between servicers cause errors that damage borrowers' credit scores and report recommendations within two years.

analysis.who_pays: Federal student loan servicing companies, which would face stricter vetting, mandatory remedies for their own errors, extended recordkeeping (at least three years after a loan closes or transfers), and the possibility of losing their contracts for misrepresentations. The Department of Education would carry new vetting, review, and reporting duties, and forbearance periods counted toward forgiveness would add modest cost to federal loan programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan servicing companies and the Education Department

drawbacks.text: The requirements apply only to contracts signed 90 days after enactment, so borrowers' immediate protections would depend on how quickly the Department rewrote its contracts and how strictly it chose to review existing 'legacy' contracts, which it would only have to review, not replace.

The remedies required of servicers—no-interest forbearance, fee reimbursement, forgiveness credit for lost time—raise the cost of servicing federal loans, and some of that cost would ultimately flow back to the government through contract prices.

Stricter vetting and revocation authority concentrate discretion with the Education Secretary; a fair-minded reading is that this could be applied unevenly or used to favor some vendors over others, which the bill's own report-to-Congress requirement (covering the Department's compliance) only partially polices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is sound: it makes the companies paid to manage borrowers' loans bear the cost of their own mistakes instead of the borrowers. The main honest weaknesses are timing (protections phase in through new contracts, leaving existing contracts to a review rather than a rewrite) and cost, since mandatory remediation will be priced into servicing contracts. The Comptroller General study is a useful diagnostic but would not by itself fix anything.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee for its entire life: introduced June 7, 2024, referred to committee the same day, and never scheduled for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Sara Jacobs introduced the bill on June 7, 2024, joined by 18 original cosponsors including Representative James Clyburn, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The cosponsor list grew to 24, all Democrats; no Republican signed on at any point.
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no report, according to the bill's complete action history.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal student loan servicing companies, which kept their contracts under existing terms with no new vetting, no mandatory remedies for their errors, and no risk of revocation for misrepresenting themselves to the Department. Borrowers left with damaged credit or lost forgiveness time from servicer mistakes remain on their own.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan servicers, who kept their contracts unchanged

industries.note: The bill would subject these companies (paid by the Department to process and collect federal student loans) to performance-based vetting, mandatory no-interest forbearance and refunds when they err, and contract revocation for lying during vetting. Their interest in keeping contracts on current terms ran against borrowers who pay the price of servicing errors.

Servicers would be required to make credit bureaus remove delinquencies caused by servicer errors, forcing bureaus to purge negative data they would otherwise hold and sell. Borrowers whose reports were damaged by someone else's mistake would get relief.
